I donno. At the time video games were so new, expensive and esoteric, and people were still poo pooing the idea that home computers, of any sort, would catch on.

It seems inevitable now that video games weren't going anywhere. But at the time they could have ended up like pogs. Or Tickle Me Elmo. Or any number of other consumer fads.

Analysts at the time could see that the struggles of the home video game market were due to corporate mismanagement and complacency. The tech was sound, there was demand for it, and there was limitless potential for progression and evolution, but all the major players were treating it like an evolved technology with nowhere else to go. People in the know would have been rightly questioning the future of home video games and home computing in general if it had looked like the tech had simply capped out its usefulness, but they all knew better. The market needed a correction to allow room for new blood to come in and treat it like a long-term, progressive opportunity, and that's what ultimately happened.

My concern, however, is primarily for the implications of this article on current views on gaming. This subverse is absolutely loaded with people who get tired and give up at the title. They won't read articles or watch videos. They'll read a sensationalist title like this one and think it's an article predicting a present-day market crash, and all of a sudden they, "watched a video explaining how <all the things they hate about gaming> are going to lead to a crash and the death of video games" if things don't change. Which of course is not in any way true.
